documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT — ESTABLISH CARE

29 y/o woman transferring primary care to us after years at another office. No acute concerns today; mainly wants a doctor she can reach.

Current issues she brings:
- Migraine without aura. Long-standing. Typical attacks a few times a month at most; sumatriptan 50 mg at onset takes care of nearly all of them, rarely needs the second dose. No change in pattern, no neuro symptoms with them.
- Acne vulgaris since her teens. Not on any prescription treatment, not much bothering her right now.
- Takes hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, prescribed by her previous PCP. Tolerating it.

No breathing, nasal or sinus complaints. Mood good, no anxiety concerns raised. PHQ-9 = 2.

MEDS (bottles reviewed): sumatriptan 50 mg PRN (max 200 mg/day); hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
ALLERGIES: NKDA.
PMH: as above. PSH: none.
FH: mother with SLE. Father with asthma and seasonal allergies. Sister with major depressive disorder.
SH: Graphic designer, schedule is flexible. Lives in Chicopee. Never smoker. Alcohol 1-2 drinks a month. No recreational or illicit drug use.
GYN: last cervical cytology at her prior office in 2020, told it was normal; will confirm from records.
VACCINES: COVID Pfizer x2 (4/9 and 4/30/2021, card reviewed). No Tdap she can recall in the last 10 years.

EXAM
BP 101/64, HR 83, RR 15, T 36.9, SpO2 98% RA. Wt 65.4 kg, Ht 166.2 cm, BMI 23.7.
Well appearing. HEENT: normal, nasal passages clear. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement or nodes. Lungs clear throughout. Heart: RRR, S1 S2 normal, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities: no edema. Skin: a few scattered comedones and small papules on the forehead and chin, no scarring. Neuro: grossly nonfocal. Mood and affect normal.

A/P
1. Establishing care. Records release signed. Baseline CBC and CMP today.
2. Migraine without aura — well controlled with as-needed sumatriptan. Refill when due.
3. Acne vulgaris — mild, no treatment wanted now. Revisit if it flares.
4. HCTZ 25 mg daily — continue, refills through us.
5. Prevention: one-time HIV and hepatitis C screening drawn today. Tdap given today. COVID series complete. Flu shot in the fall. Cervical screening next due 2023 if the 2020 result is confirmed normal.
6. Yearly physicals here going forward; message any time.

Seen with MA for rooming and vaccine.

reports.text: Pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry performed in office. Patient effort good; maneuvers acceptable. Pre-bronchodilator: obstructive pattern, with variability between efforts. Post-bronchodilator (albuterol 4 puffs via spacer, repeat at 15 min): significant improvement in airflow meeting standard reversibility criteria (at least 12% and 200 mL).
reports.conclusion: Variable airflow obstruction with a significant bronchodilator response, consistent with asthma.

documents.title: Office Visit — breathing, nasal symptoms
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: chest tightness and shortness of breath on and off for about 6 months.

HPI: 30 y/o F. Since last summer, intermittent episodes of feeling short of breath with tightness across the chest. Most often in the early morning, and some nights it wakes her. Cold air outside and strong smells (cleaning products, perfume) can bring it on. No fever, no sputum, no weight loss. A friend gave her an over-the-counter pill that helps for a few hours and then it comes back; she doesn't know what it was.
Also: nose stuffed up most of the time with a lot of sneezing; she says spring and fall are the worst.
Never smoker. No drugs. Father has asthma.

Meds: sumatriptan 50 mg PRN, HCTZ 25 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 107/71, HR 79, RR 14, T 36.9, SpO2 98% RA. Wt 66.3 kg.
Comfortable, talking in full sentences. Nose: mucosa mildly red and swollen, no polyps. Pharynx clear. Lungs clear, no wheeze even on forced expiration. Heart: regular rate and rhythm, normal S1/S2, no murmur. No edema.

Spirometry today (pre/post albuterol): obstruction that varies effort to effort and improves significantly after bronchodilator, meets reversibility criteria. Report in chart.

A/P
1. Mild persistent asthma — new diagnosis. Night waking and symptoms most days fit persistent, not intermittent. Exam normal between episodes. Reversible obstruction on spirometry.
 - Start montelukast 10 mg nightly as controller. Reviewed the FDA warning: stop it and call if she notices mood changes, unusual dreams or sleep trouble, or anything that feels off psychologically.
 - Albuterol HFA 90 mcg, 1-2 puffs q4-6h PRN. Taught inhaler technique with spacer.
 - Avoid triggers where she can. Asked her not to take the friend's pill anymore.
 - Telehealth check in about 6 weeks.
2. Nasal congestion and sneezing, seasonal worsening — likely allergic rhinitis. Mucosa red and swollen today. Referred to ENT for evaluation. Allergy list unchanged for now.
3. Migraine, HCTZ — no change.

Return sooner or go to the ED for breathlessness not relieved by albuterol.

documents.title: After Visit Summary
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Today we diagnosed mild persistent asthma.

New medicines:
- Montelukast 10 mg, one tablet every night. This is your daily controller. If you notice changes in mood, sleep or unusual dreams, stop it and message us.
- Albuterol inhaler, 1-2 puffs every 4-6 hours when you're tight or short of breath. Use with the spacer.

Please don't take the pill your friend gave you.

We're sending you to ENT for your nose.

We'll check in by video in about 6 weeks. If albuterol isn't helping or you're struggling to breathe, call 911 or go to the ED.

documents.author: otolaryngology
documents.body:
OTOLARYNGOLOGY — CONSULTATION LETTER
Date of service: 04/13/2022
Referred by: primary care

Reason for referral: chronic nasal congestion and sneezing.

Ms. Williams is a 30 year old woman seen today at the request of her primary care physician, about three months after the visit at which she was diagnosed with mild persistent asthma. Since early spring she has had three weeks of itchy eyes, sneezing and a blocked nose that runs clear. She tells me the same thing happens every year around this time and hangs on until the spring is over. Store-bought antihistamine tablets have done very little.

Medications: albuterol inhaler as needed.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Social: never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks per month; graphic designer.

Examination: vital signs within normal limits. Nasal lining pale and boggy with a thin clear drip bilaterally. No tenderness over the maxillary or frontal sinuses. Oropharynx clear. Lungs clear to auscultation.

Impression: Seasonal allergic rhinitis. The timing, recurring each early spring, points to tree and grass pollens. I have added seasonal tree and grass pollen allergy to her record. Formal allergy testing was not performed today.

Plan: She will continue an over-the-counter oral antihistamine through the season. No new prescription today. Return to clinic as needed.

Thank you for allowing me to see her.

Otolaryngology

Washes her hands many times a day and cleans the apartment over and over to settle the fear. She knows it's more than it should be. It's eating into her day and she's embarrassed by it. Not depressed; PHQ-9 = 3. No thoughts of self-harm. No alcohol increase, no drugs.

Asthma: fine. Albuterol rarely. Still on montelukast nightly.

Meds: montelukast 10 mg nightly, albuterol HFA PRN, sumatriptan 50 mg PRN, HCTZ 25 mg daily.

A/P
1. Contamination fears with washing/cleaning rituals — sounds obsessive-compulsive in character. Referring to psychiatry for diagnosis and treatment; she's open to it. Gave crisis line info though no safety concerns today.
2. Mild persistent asthma — montelukast carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects. I'm not saying it caused this, but with new psychiatric symptoms I'd rather take it off the table. Stopping montelukast. Starting fluticasone HFA 44 mcg, 2 puffs twice daily, rinse after. Albuterol PRN unchanged. Video check in about 2 months.
3. Others unchanged.

OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY — INITIAL EVALUATION
Date of service: 03/09/2023
Referral source: primary care

Identifying data: 31 year old woman, graphic designer, with mild persistent asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, both evaluated last year (primary care and ENT).

Chief concern: fear of germs.

History: For about six months she has been troubled by intrusive worries that she will pick up germs and become ill. To quiet the fear she washes her hands and cleans her home, and this now takes several hours of each day. She is clear that the fear is out of proportion and does not make sense to her, yet she cannot keep herself from acting on it. No prior psychiatric treatment. Denies alcohol misuse or any substance use.

Medications: albuterol inhaler as needed; fluticasone inhaler twice daily; sumatriptan as needed; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
Allergies: no known drug allergies; seasonal pollens.
Family history: mother with SLE; father with asthma and seasonal allergies; sister with major depressive disorder.

Vitals: within normal limits.
Exam: skin of both hands dry, cracked and reddened.
Mental status: casually dressed, cooperative, anxious affect, speech normal, thought process linear, content notable for contamination obsessions with insight intact. No suicidal or homicidal ideation. No psychotic features.

Labs today: CBC, TSH and basic metabolic panel all within normal limits.

Diagnosis: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, contamination type, with good insight.

Plan:
1. Start sertraline 50 mg daily. Discussed expected time to benefit, GI upset early on, and to call with any worsening anxiety or suicidal thoughts.
2. Follow up in clinic in about six months; sooner as needed.

Psychiatry

documents.title: Psychiatry follow-up
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT PSYCHIATRY — FOLLOW-UP
Date of service: 09/05/2023

32 year old woman with obsessive-compulsive disorder (contamination), mild persistent asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, last seen here six months ago and started on sertraline 50 mg.

Interval: The contamination rituals have settled; she denies any current compulsions. What brings her in now is something broader. For the last 10 to 12 months she has felt wound up nearly all the time, including on days when nothing is going wrong. Small things spiral into worst-case thinking: whether the curling iron is still plugged in, whether a tire will blow out on a short drive across town. Most nights she lies awake a long time before sleep comes, and she wakes in the night running lists and imagining disasters. In the daytime she is tired and her concentration at work has slipped; tension headaches are more frequent. Her job allows flexible hours, but she is drained by midday. She has started skipping team meetings, worried that colleagues will judge her if she forgets to contribute something.

She took three weeks away this summer hoping a change of scene would help: visiting friends in Colorado, driving through national parks in Utah, and ending at a desert pottery retreat in Arizona. She enjoyed parts of it, but the worry came along. When a friend's dog developed diarrhea, she spent hours online looking up after-hours animal hospitals.

She goes to a pottery studio twice a week and finds it calming when she can focus. She has more than 200 regional hot sauces on shelves in her kitchen. She recently started buying contemporary art online, which has been more stressful than she expected. In a stable relationship. Drinks socially, no recreational drugs.

ROS: no panic attacks, no hallucinations, no flashbacks. Appetite normal. Notices a clenched jaw and some queasiness on her worst days.

Mental status: mildly restless, cooperative, affect appropriate, thought process logical and goal-directed. No suicidal ideation.

Assessment:
1. Generalized anxiety disorder.
2. Obsessive-compulsive disorder, compulsions currently in remission on sertraline.

Plan: She agrees to treatment and would like to avoid anything sedating or habit-forming. Increase sertraline to 100 mg daily. Sleep hygiene reviewed. Follow up in about six months, sooner as needed.

Psychiatry

documents.title: Painful rash after beach weekend
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Pt called first thing. Spent the weekend at a beach resort. Since yesterday her face and forearms are red and painful, some small blisters. No trouble breathing, no swelling of lips or tongue, mouth and eyes fine, no fever. Started doxycycline 10/8. Want dermatology eyes on this today or tomorrow. Called their urgent line and got her in tomorrow morning. Told her: cool compresses, stay out of the sun, call back or go to urgent care if it spreads, blisters widely, involves her mouth or eyes, or she feels sick.

REGIONAL HOSPITAL — NEPHROLOGY ADMISSION HISTORY AND PHYSICAL
Admitted: 06/30/2025
Referring: primary care (urgent)

Chief complaint: three weeks of fatigue, joint pain and leg swelling, with a new facial rash.

HPI: 33 year old woman with prior hydrochlorothiazide-induced photosensitivity (October 2024). For three weeks she has felt run down, with aching joints and swollen legs. She has also developed a red rash across both cheeks that gets worse with sun. No recent infections. No travel. Her PCP found blood, protein and casts in the urine last week and called us.

PMH: mild persistent asthma; seasonal allergic rhinitis; OCD; generalized anxiety disorder; migraine without aura; acne vulgaris. Hydrochlorothiazide photosensitivity 10/2024.
PSH: none.

Home medications:
- albuterol HFA 90 mcg: 1-2 puffs q4-6h PRN
- fluticasone propionate HFA 44 mcg, 2 puffs twice daily
- sertraline 100 mg daily
- sumatriptan 50 mg as needed (max 200 mg/day)
- hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily: STOPPED 10/2024 (photosensitivity)
She uses her albuterol inhaler only occasionally.

Allergies: seasonal pollens (tree, grass); hydrochlorothiazide (photosensitivity).

Family history: mother with SLE; father with asthma and seasonal allergies; sister with major depressive disorder.
Social: never smoker; alcohol 1-2 drinks per month; graphic designer.

Exam: BP 145/90, HR 86, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 98% RA.
General: fatigued, no distress. Skin: erythematous malar rash. Lungs clear. Heart regular, no rub, no murmur. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities: bilateral pitting edema to the shins. Joints: no synovitis.

Labs (6/30): urinalysis with protein and blood, red blood cell casts on microscopy. Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL. Albumin 2.8 g/dL. 24-hour urine protein 4.5 g. ANA positive.

Assessment: active urine sediment with heavy proteinuria, low albumin, edema and raised blood pressure, together with a photosensitive malar rash and arthralgia. Strong concern for lupus nephritis.

Plan: complement levels and anti-dsDNA sent. Kidney biopsy 7/1. Given the proteinuria and active sediment, IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily x 3 days started 6/30 after discussion with the patient. Daily weights, low salt diet.

ADDENDUM 07/01/2025 08:40: C3 low. C4 low. Anti-dsDNA positive. With the positive ANA, this is systemic lupus erythematosus presenting with a lupus nephritis flare. Rheumatology aware. Biopsy proceeding today.

documents.title: Emergency department provider note
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT — PROVIDER NOTE
Arrival: 03/12/2026 18:05, brought in by friends.

HPI: 34 year old woman brought in for strange behavior after spending the day at an outdoor music festival. Friends say she was dancing wildly, kept saying she was overheating, and drank very little water. History is limited by agitation; obtained from friends and, later, the patient. Medications include sertraline and sumatriptan, and she takes an over-the-counter dextromethorphan cough syrup now and then for a long-standing throat irritation. She has lupus and is on immunosuppressive therapy. Friends deny alcohol or drugs at the festival; patient later confirms.

PMH: anxiety/OCD, migraine, asthma, SLE with kidney involvement.
Home medications (from our system): albuterol HFA as needed; fluticasone HFA 44 mcg 2 puffs twice daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily.
Allergies: seasonal pollens; no known drug allergies.

Exam: T 39.7 C (103.5 F), HR 120, BP 168/94, RR 24, SpO2 97% RA.
Awake, agitated, intermittently combative. Pupils dilated. Profuse sweating. Bowel sounds increased. Neuro: inducible clonus at both ankles, hyperreflexia in both lower extremities, mild rigidity. Neck supple. No photophobia. Lungs clear. Heart tachycardic, regular. No rash.
Fingerstick glucose normal.

MDM: Clinical picture of serotonin toxicity (clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, agitation, mydriasis, diaphoresis) in a patient on sertraline and sumatriptan with dextromethorphan use, plus heat and dehydration. Because she is immunosuppressed and febrile, infection was evaluated as well: CBC, CMP, CK, urinalysis, blood and urine cultures and chest x-ray.

Results: CBC normal. CMP normal, creatinine 0.9. CK normal. Urinalysis bland. Chest x-ray clear. Cultures pending.

Treatment: active external cooling, IV fluids, IV benzodiazepine for agitation, cyproheptadine by mouth (loading dose, then scheduled). Sertraline and sumatriptan held. Dextromethorphan stopped.

Course: by 22:00 temperature 37.6, HR 94, calmer, clonus diminishing.

Diagnosis: serotonin syndrome.
Disposition: ED observation overnight.

Emergency Medicine

documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
ED OBSERVATION — DISCHARGE NOTE
Observation 03/12/2026 to 03/13/2026

Diagnosis: serotonin syndrome.

Course: cooled, IV fluids, benzodiazepine and cyproheptadine. Temperature normal since midnight. Agitation resolved; alert and oriented, appropriate. Clonus resolved on morning exam; reflexes normal. Tolerating food and fluids. 10:30 vitals: T 36.8, HR 76, BP 120/76, RR 16, SpO2 99%.
Blood and urine cultures no growth so far; final results to PCP.

Instructions:
- Do NOT take dextromethorphan (in many cough and cold products).
- Hold sertraline and sumatriptan until reviewed by your PCP and psychiatrist.
- Hydrate, rest, avoid heat today.
- Follow up with PCP within 1 week.
- Return for fever, confusion, muscle stiffness or twitching.
